chapter_metadata.chapter_title: Writing prescriptions and understanding dosage forms
tags: Writing prescriptions and understanding dosage forms

sections.section_title: Writing prescriptions and understanding dosage forms

blocks.text: This chapter focuses on how to translate a clinical decision into a complete, unambiguous and safe prescription. It covers prescription components, dosage forms, routes of administration, frequency, duration, quantity calculations, medication orders and common prescribing errors.
A prescription is a legal and clinical instruction for the supply and/or administration of a medicine. Its precise requirements depend on the country, medicine classification and clinical setting.

blocks.title: A complete prescription should answer six questions:

items.text: What medicine? Generic name and, where necessary, the specific formulation.
How much medicine is in each unit? Strength and dosage form.
How much should the patient receive? Dose per administration.
How should it be given? Route and administration instructions.
How often and for how long? Frequency, duration and stop/review plan.
How much should be supplied? Total quantity to dispense.

blocks.text: It should also identify the patient and prescriber, include the date, and satisfy applicable documentation and legal requirements.
The following is an educational example, not a recommendation for a particular patient.
SAMPLE OUTPATIENT PRESCRIPTION
Patient: Example Adult
Date: 20 October 2026
Medicine: Paracetamol
Dosage form and strength: Tablet, 500 mg
Dose: 500 mg per administration
Route: Oral
Frequency: Every 6 hours when required for pain
Duration: Up to 3 days, followed by reassessment if pain persists
Quantity: 12 tablets
Additional instructions: Do not exceed the prescribed maximum daily dose. Check other medicines for paracetamol/acetaminophen content.
Prescriber: Name, registration details and signature as required.

The maximum safe dose depends on factors such as age, body weight, liver disease, nutritional status, alcohol use and other paracetamol-containing products. The example's regimen must be assessed against those factors before use.

subsections.subsection_title: 2.2 The difference between medicine name, strength, dose and dosage form

blocks.text: These terms are frequently confused in examinations and clinical practice.
Medicine name
Amoxicillin
Identifies the active pharmaceutical ingredient.
Dosage form
Capsule, suspension or injection
The physical form in which the medicine is supplied.
Strength
250 mg per capsule
The amount of active ingredient contained in a specified unit or volume.
Dose
500 mg per administration
The amount of medicine the patient is instructed to receive each time.
Frequency
Every 8 hours
How often each dose is administered.
Duration
5 days
The intended length of the treatment course.
Quantity
30 capsules
The total number of dosage units supplied.
Suppose a hypothetical prescription specifies 500 mg per dose, using 250 mg capsules, three times daily for five days.

items.text: Capsules per dose: (500 \ 250 = 2)
Doses per day: (3)
Duration: (5) days
Total quantity: (2 x 3 x 5 = 30) capsules.

blocks.text: Dosage form affects absorption, stability, administration, adherence and sometimes the safety of the medicine.
A. Solid dosage forms

items.text: Tablets: immediate-release, chewable, dispersible, effervescent and modified-release.
Capsules: hard or soft gelatin and other capsule materials.
Powders and granules: oral solutions, suspensions or sachets.
Sublingual and buccal preparations.

blocks.text: Key safety issue: modified-release and enteric-coated preparations must not be crushed or opened unless the specific product information confirms that it is safe.
B. Liquid dosage forms

items.text: Solutions: the active ingredient is dissolved.
Suspensions: particles are dispersed in a liquid and may settle.
Syrups and other oral liquids.
Drops and concentrated oral preparations.

blocks.text: Key safety issue: verify the concentration in mg/mL, shake suspensions when instructed, and use a suitable oral syringe or measuring device.
C. Parenteral preparations

items.text: Intravenous injections and infusions.
Intramuscular and subcutaneous injections.
Intradermal preparations.
Powders requiring reconstitution before use.

blocks.text: Key safety issue: confirm the intended route, product concentration, diluent, final volume, compatibility, stability and administration rate.
D. Topical and transdermal preparations

items.text: Creams, ointments, gels and lotions.
Eye and ear preparations.
Nasal sprays.
Transdermal patches.

blocks.text: Key safety issue: specify the application site, frequency, duration and relevant precautions. A transdermal patch delivers medicine systemically and is not interchangeable with an ordinary topical preparation.
E. Inhaled preparations

items.text: Metered-dose inhalers.
Dry-powder inhalers.
Nebuliser solutions.

blocks.text: Key safety issue: specify the device and prescribed dose, check technique, and distinguish the amount delivered per actuation from the total contents of the inhaler.
F. Other dosage forms

items.text: Rectal suppositories and enemas.
Vaginal tablets, pessaries and creams.
Medicated implants and depot injections.
Intrathecal or other specialist preparations.

blocks.text: Key safety issue: the intended route must be explicit. Some specialist formulations require trained personnel and specific administration environments.
This distinction is particularly important when prescribing cardiovascular medicines, analgesics, antiepileptics and other medicines with multiple formulations.

rows: Releases the drug without a designed prolonged-release mechanism
Releases the drug over an extended period
Often has a different dosing schedule; crushing may alter drug release
Release is intentionally postponed, for example by an enteric coating
Crushing may destroy the protective mechanism
Designed to resist dissolution in the stomach
Do not crush or chew unless product-specific instructions permit it
Designed to disperse in liquid before administration
Follow the product instructions for preparation and administration

blocks.text: High-yield example: A modified-release tablet and an immediate-release tablet may contain the same total amount of active ingredient but have different dosing intervals and concentration-time profiles. Do not substitute one for the other solely because the strength looks identical.
The route affects how quickly a medicine acts, how much reaches the systemic circulation, whether it undergoes first-pass metabolism, and which administration risks must be considered.

rows: Convenient; absorption may be affected by food, vomiting, gut function and first-pass metabolism
Immediate systemic availability; risks include extravasation, infusion reactions and rapid toxicity
Absorption varies with muscle perfusion; consider bleeding risk, muscle mass and injection volume
Useful for medicines such as insulin and selected anticoagulants; absorption varies with perfusion
Used for selected tests and vaccines
Absorption through oral mucosa; the preparation must be suitable for sublingual use
May be useful when oral administration is unsuitable, but absorption can be variable
Primarily intended for local application, although systemic absorption may occur
Designed for systemic delivery through the skin over time
Drug delivery depends on the device, technique and respiratory condition
Specialist route requiring strict product and procedural safeguards
Used for local or systemic treatment, depending on the preparation

blocks.text: Always write the intended route explicitly where ambiguity could lead to harm. An injectable product is not automatically suitable for every parenteral route.
Consider a patient with an infection requiring antimicrobial treatment.

Oral treatment may be appropriate when the patient is clinically stable, can swallow and absorb medicines, and has an effective oral option available. Intravenous treatment may be needed when illness is severe, oral absorption is unreliable, the patient cannot take oral medicines, or the selected medicine requires IV administration.

The IV route is not automatically more effective for every condition. When clinically appropriate, switching from IV to oral therapy can reduce line-related complications, cost and hospital resource use.
Prescription frequency should communicate the intended schedule clearly.

rows: Specify a particular time if timing matters
Often spaced approximately 12 hours apart, if appropriate for the medicine
Does not necessarily mean exactly every 8 hours
Important when maintaining a defined dosing interval
Check for sedation, falls risk and other relevant precautions
Administer before meals according to product-specific instructions
The required interval varies between medicines
Administer with or after a meal as specified
May improve tolerability or alter absorption
Administer only when the stated indication occurs
Specify the indication, minimum interval and maximum dose

content_groups.group_title: Is three times daily the same as every 8 hours?

blocks.text: No.

items.text: Three times daily commonly means three administrations during the patient's waking day.
Every 8 hours means the doses are separated by 8-hour intervals.

blocks.text: This distinction can be important for medicines whose efficacy or toxicity depends on maintaining a particular concentration over time.

items.text: The indication, such as pain or nausea.
The dose per administration.
The route.
The minimum interval between doses.
The maximum dose over the specified period.
Any special precautions and when reassessment is required.

blocks.text: For example, an order that states only “analgesia PRN” is incomplete because it does not identify the medicine or the permitted dose.
Scheduled medicines are given at defined times. PRN medicines are given only when the stated indication exists and the dose is safe.

Do not convert a scheduled medicine to PRN, or vice versa, without considering the clinical indication. This is especially important for antiseizure medicines, corticosteroids, anticoagulants, insulin and medicines that may cause withdrawal symptoms.

subsections.subsection_title: 2.7 Duration of treatment and stopping medicines

blocks.text: The duration must be based on the indication, evidence, patient response and relevant guideline.

items.text: Antibiotics: duration depends on the infection, severity, source control and applicable guideline.
Analgesics: use the shortest appropriate course and reassess persistent pain.
Corticosteroids: some courses require tapering, while others can be stopped without tapering; the decision depends on dose, duration, indication and patient factors.
Anticoagulants: duration depends on the indication and the balance between thrombosis and bleeding risks.
Chronic medicines: specify ongoing review and criteria for modification or discontinuation.
Emergency medicines: document the immediate indication, monitoring and subsequent treatment plan.

blocks.text: Never use an arbitrary duration simply because it is customary for another condition.
Deprescribing is the planned, supervised reduction or discontinuation of medicines when their risks outweigh their benefits or their indication has resolved.

items.text: Whether the original indication remains valid.
Whether the medicine is still effective.
Whether the patient is experiencing adverse effects.
Whether withdrawal or rebound effects are possible.
Whether dose reduction, substitution or monitoring is needed.

blocks.text: Stopping a medicine is a prescribing decision too.

The quantity required is 14 tablets.

content_groups.group_title: Worked example 2: multiple tablets per dose

blocks.text: A hypothetical prescription specifies two tablets three times daily for five days.
The quantity required is 30 tablets.
A hypothetical medicine is prescribed at 5 mL three times daily for five days.

The calculated treatment volume is 75 mL. The quantity actually dispensed must account for the available bottle sizes, product instructions and any justified additional volume required for accurate measurement.
For variable-dose tapers, loading regimens, PRN medicines and partial courses, calculate the quantity from the actual dosing schedule rather than applying the basic formula blindly.
This is one of the most important skills in paediatrics.

content_groups.group_title: Why concentration must always be checked

blocks.text: Suppose the intended dose is 250 mg.

items.text: At 125 mg/5 mL, the volume is 10 mL.
At 250 mg/5 mL, the volume is 5 mL.

blocks.text: Giving 10 mL of the second preparation would deliver 500 mg, twice the intended dose.
Paediatric safety rule

Before administering an oral liquid, verify the prescribed dose in mg, the actual bottle concentration, the calculated volume in mL and the appropriate measuring device. Do not estimate doses using household teaspoons.
For a suspension, follow the product instructions on shaking and preparation. If the product requires reconstitution, verify the final concentration and beyond-use instructions after preparation.
Injectable medicines need particular attention because errors in dose, concentration, dilution and administration rate can cause rapid harm.

blocks.title: An injectable order may need to specify:

items.text: Medicine and formulation.
Dose in the appropriate unit.
Route.
Diluent and volume, where applicable.
Final concentration or total volume.
Administration rate or duration.
Frequency and indication.
Compatibility requirements.
Monitoring and relevant precautions.

content_groups.group_title: Example of a structured IV order

blocks.text: ILLUSTRATIVE ORDER FORMAT
Medicine: [Generic name]
Dose: [Required amount and unit]
Route: Intravenous
Preparation: [Approved diluent, volume and final concentration, as appropriate]
Administration: [Approved rate or infusion duration]
Frequency: [Specified schedule]
Monitoring: [Relevant observations, laboratory tests and adverse effects]
The bracketed fields must be completed using the specific product information and applicable protocol. This template is not an instruction to prepare or administer an unspecified IV medicine.
These terms describe different processes.

items.text: Reconstitution: Adding a specified diluent to a powder or concentrated product to prepare it for use.
Dilution: Reducing a solution's concentration by adding a compatible diluent.
Infusion: Administering a prepared solution over a specified period.

blocks.text: The correct diluent, amount, final concentration, stability and storage requirements are medicine-specific. Do not assume that normal saline, sterile water and dextrose solutions are interchangeable.
For an infusion delivered by a pump:
Example: If an approved infusion contains 500 mL and is intended to run over 4 hours:
The pump rate is 125 mL/hour, assuming the prescription and fluid plan are clinically appropriate.
For gravity infusions:
The giving-set factor must be obtained from the actual equipment. Never assume all IV giving sets deliver the same number of drops per millilitre.

subsections.subsection_title: 2.11 Prescription auditing: how to check a prescription before signing

blocks.text: Prescription auditing is the systematic review of a prescription for clinical appropriateness, completeness, legality and safety.
Use this framework when reviewing your own prescriptions, another clinician's orders or a medication chart.

rows: Is the medicine needed for this diagnosis?
Is it the preferred medicine for this patient?
Has the allergy history been reviewed?
Is the dose correct for the indication and patient?
Does the available product match the intended dose?
Is the medicine suitable for the prescribed route?
Is the schedule appropriate for the medicine?
Is there a clear stop date or review plan?
Could another medicine increase toxicity or reduce efficacy?
Is there a reason the medicine should be avoided?
Are the required tests and observations arranged?
Is the amount to dispense consistent with the regimen?
Can the pharmacist, nurse and patient understand the instructions?

blocks.text: If an order is unclear or potentially unsafe, clarify it with the prescriber before administration, following local policy. Do not guess the intended dose or silently alter a prescription.
A prescription may be clinically correct but still lead to harm if the patient does not understand how to use the medicine.
A dispensing label should provide the medicine identity and clear directions consistent with the applicable legal requirements.

blocks.title: Counselling should cover the following where relevant:

items.text: What the medicine treats and what benefit to expect.
How much to take and when to take it.
Whether it should be taken with food or on an empty stomach.
How to measure liquids or use inhalers, injections and other devices.
Important side effects and warning signs.
What to do after a missed dose.
Whether alcohol, driving or particular activities require precautions.
How to store the medicine.
When to return for review and when to seek urgent care.

blocks.text: Avoid giving a blanket instruction to double the next dose after a missed dose. The correct advice depends on the medicine and how close the patient is to the next scheduled dose.

content_groups.group_title: A. Patients who cannot swallow tablets

blocks.text: Consider an appropriate alternative formulation, such as a liquid, dispersible tablet or another suitable route.

Do not automatically crush tablets or open capsules. Modified-release and enteric-coated preparations may be unsafe to crush, and some capsules must remain intact for correct absorption. Certain medicines can also expose the person preparing them to hazardous drug particles. Check product-specific guidance and consult a pharmacist when necessary.

content_groups.group_title: B. Medicines administered through feeding tubes

blocks.text: Check whether the medicine is suitable for the particular tube and administration method.

items.text: Whether an alternative formulation is available.
Whether the medicine can be crushed or dispersed.
Tube blockage and drug adsorption risks.
Interactions with enteral feeds.
Whether feeds need to be paused.
How to flush the tube safely according to the relevant protocol.

blocks.text: Do not mix several medicines together in a feeding tube unless compatibility and administration instructions have been established.

Medicines with similar names or packaging can be confused. Reduce the risk by checking the complete medicine name, strength, dosage form, indication and label rather than relying on packaging appearance.
The WHO identifies high-risk medicines, polypharmacy and transitions of care as important priorities for preventing medication-related harm.

blocks.title: At discharge, reconcile the inpatient and outpatient medication lists. Explicitly identify:

items.text: Medicines to continue.
Medicines to start.
Medicines whose doses have changed.
Medicines that have been stopped.
Temporary medicines and their stop dates.
Monitoring and follow-up arrangements.

blocks.text: This is particularly important after acute kidney injury, surgery, pregnancy-related admissions and changes to anticoagulant or insulin regimens.

Three doses at any time during the day
A dose every 8 hours
A dose only at bedtime
